Samsung unveiled a multi-pronged approach to topple what it calls the digital memory wall created by AI workloads, outlining a 3D memory roadmap that includes advances in both high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and NAND flash.

In a pre-briefing ahead of a public keynote at this week’s Future of Memory and Storage Summit, Leno Park, VP of flash solutions at Samsung Electronics, laid out the company’s multi-generation memory roadmap built around 3D architectures, tighter integration with AI accelerators, and a series of process and packaging advances. He said the roadmap is designed to keep pace with workloads that the company expects will require 10× more token throughput by the end of the decade.

Park said current AI infrastructure is already straining to support roughly 100 tokens per second per user in 2026, but Samsung is planning for a much steeper curve. “By the year 2030, we expect 1,000 tokens per second per user,” he claimed.

Moving toward fully 3D HBM

It should come as no surprise that HBM4E is front and center in Samsung’s AI strategy, which also includes new cooling technology and a move to true 3D stacking.

Park said HBM4E is now in the sampling phase, with major ecosystem partners evaluating the devices. Park described the product as an important step in an especially compressed development timeline. “The HBM development cycle is really, really fast and [has] accelerated more than ever,” he said, adding that HBM is expected to account for more than 50% of DRAM sales in 2030.

Park said Samsung’s HBM design uses a 4‑nm base die, increases the number of internal through-silicon vias (TSVs) by about 4×, and employs advanced packaging with more than 300,000 microbumps and smaller joint pitches to improve reliability and thermal management.

He said Samsung is targeting another generational leap with HBM5 by using a 2‑nm base die built on gate-all-around (GAA) transistor technology and shortening interposer channel lengths to improve I/O signaling between the base die and the accelerator.

Samsung is also introducing a new thermal mechanism the company calls a heat pipe block, which Park described as a kind of “chimney” over hot spots in the HBM stack to help dissipate heat more efficiently and cool the HBM.

The company also used FMS as an opportunity to introduce zHBM, a concept that moves from the current 2.5D side‑by‑side layout. “We are going to put them into [the] accelerator over to the HBM stack as a single kind of a structure, as a true 3D domain zone,” Park said.

By placing the AI accelerator directly over the HBM stack rather than alongside it, the distance data must travel between processor and memory is shortened. This architecture is expected to improve bandwidth and power efficiency while reducing thermal constraints.

Samsung claimed a next‑generation interface incorporating zHBM could deliver roughly 8× the performance of HBM5, more than 10× the memory density, 3× the energy efficiency, and less than half the thermal resistance. Park said realizing those gains will require close co‑design with accelerator partners.

zNAND-O targets edge AI bottlenecks

HBM, which is essentially stacked synchronous DRAM, is not the only technology Samsung is using to overcome the digital memory wall.

The company’s zHBM announcement was complemented by zNAND-O, a next-generation NAND concept aimed at edge AI and other data-intensive environments. Built on Samsung’s V‑NAND technology, the architecture is designed to combine high space efficiency with improved I/O performance, power efficiency, and lower latency by shortening the distance data must travel between processor and memory.

Park said the 10th generation of Samsung’s TLC V-NAND will have more than 400-layer counts and 11% lateral shrink while memory density has increased by approximately 58%. Park said AI models are getting bigger and that the conventional memory architecture won’t be able to keep up—the industry is approaching a wall that will require a structural change in design rather than another routine speed bump. “After 2029, we need some breakthrough technology to overcome digital memory wall,” he said.
